global.headline: IRAN — SECOND NIGHT OF US STRIKES HITS 90 TARGETS, BUSHEHR PERIMETER; TEHRAN RETALIATES AGAINST BAHRAIN, KUWAIT, QATAR AND JORDAN
summary: CENTCOM completed a second wave of strikes overnight July 8-9, hitting roughly 90 Iranian military targets along the country's coast — air-defence systems, coastal surveillance equipment, missile and drone storage and maintenance sites, naval assets and logistics infrastructure — following the July 7-8 opening wave that hit about 80 targets, including more than 60 IRGC fast-attack craft. Iran's Bushehr deputy governor said a US projectile struck the perimeter of the Bushehr nuclear power plant; Iranian state media also reported strikes on the Aq Taqeh Khan railway bridge in Golestan province — a rail link to strategic partners China and Russia — and said Tehran-Mashhad rail operations were halted. Iran's Health Ministry said at least 14 people were killed and 78 injured (47 still hospitalised) across five provinces.

Iran retaliated in two phases. Its army/IRGC first launched drone and missile attacks on a Patriot air-defence battery in Kuwait, a satellite and early-warning site in Qatar, and fuel-storage facilities used by US forces in Bahrain. It then fired ten ballistic missiles at Jordan's Al Azraq air base, which hosts US, German, Belgian and French personnel; Jordan said it intercepted eight, with no casualties or damage. Kuwait's military said it shot down three ballistic missiles, a cruise missile and ten drones, with one person wounded by falling debris.

Oil pulled back from July 8's surge as markets weighed the uncertainty: Brent fell $1.03 to $76.99 a barrel and WTI dropped $0.88 to $72.64 by 07:49 GMT on July 9, with vessel-tracking data showing fewer Hormuz transits but continued movement along Iran-approved routes. Trump said the US would "probably" strike again and repeated that Washington could take Kharg Island outright and reimpose a full blockade. Pakistani, Qatari, Egyptian, Turkish and Saudi mediators continued working around the clock to keep the MOU from collapsing entirely; New Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei's prolonged public absence remains the central unresolved signal of who is actually directing Iran's response.
global.geopolitical: The conflict's geographic footprint widened sharply overnight — from a US-Iran exchange centred on Hormuz to strikes on four Gulf-adjacent states' territory in a single day — raising the odds that Kuwait, Qatar, Bahrain or Jordan get drawn more directly into a war none of them are party to. That five-country mediation effort held together through the funeral period is itself notable; whether it can hold through a second consecutive night of large-scale strikes is now the operative question, with Mojtaba Khamenei's continued silence leaving Iran's actual chain of command opaque to everyone involved.
global.socioeconomic: A second consecutive day of double-digit-target strikes keeps the crisis compounding on every front already tracked in this briefing: Hormuz reopening pushed further out, the record Q3 electricity tariff's conflict-era gas costs, and STB's downgraded tourism forecast. The rail strike on the China/Russia trade link is a new node of disruption distinct from the maritime one. For Singapore specifically, the pattern (strikes spreading to more states, oil pulling back rather than spiking further) suggests markets are still pricing containment over collapse — a read that could reverse quickly given Trump's stated intent to keep striking.

global.headline: LEBANON, GAZA CEASEFIRES FRAY FURTHER: ISRAELI STRIKES KILL 2 IN NABATIEH, AT LEAST 9 PALESTINIANS IN GAZA INCLUDING AID DRIVER
summary: An Israeli drone strike killed two people in Nabatieh, southern Lebanon on July 8, Lebanon's National News Agency said — the latest in a series of strikes Lebanese officials say violate the ceasefire that took effect June 21 as part of the broader US-brokered regional framework. Israel maintains the strikes are responses to ongoing Hezbollah activity in the area; Netanyahu has said Israeli forces will remain in southern Lebanon "indefinitely."

In Gaza, health officials reported at least nine Palestinians killed by Israeli airstrikes and gunfire over the preceding 24 hours, including Ahmad Nasser Saleem, a driver delivering food for World Central Kitchen, whose vehicle was struck while transporting goods from the Karem Abu Salem crossing. A separate missile strike hit a displaced-persons tent in Khan Younis's al-Mawasi area, killing at least four people, including a ten-year-old child. World Central Kitchen said "humanitarian aid deliveries should never be a target."
global.geopolitical: Both fronts show how selectively the region's ceasefire architecture is holding even as its Gulf-facing dimension is actively collapsing elsewhere in this briefing — Lebanon's truce and Gaza's have each been violated repeatedly since signing, with no enforcement mechanism visibly changing that pattern. Gaza's governance handoff (Emergency Committee dissolved July 6, NCAG still based outside Gaza) remains stalled independent of today's violence.
global.socioeconomic: Primarily humanitarian rather than market-moving; the immediate cost falls on aid-delivery organisations and displaced civilians rather than the broader region's economic indicators tracked elsewhere in this briefing.

global.headline: NATO'S ANKARA SUMMIT CLOSES: US LIFTS TURKEY SANCTIONS, TRUMP MOVES TO STRIKE SYRIA FROM TERROR-SPONSOR LIST
summary: NATO's Ankara summit concluded July 9 with Trump praising the alliance's "unity," per a readout from outgoing UK Prime Minister Keir Starmer, even as European members brace for further friction with Washington ahead. Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan told a closing press conference that the US had largely lifted defence sanctions against Turkey, and said he and Trump had discussed joint defence-industrial cooperation, including possible shipbuilding — frigates and submarines.

On the summit sidelines, Trump held a bilateral meeting with Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa and formally notified Congress of his intent to rescind Syria's designation as a State Sponsor of Terrorism — a listing in place since 1979 — opening a 45-day congressional review period. The move follows Trump's June 2025 executive order on Syria sanctions relief and assurances from al-Sharaa's government that Syria will not support international terrorism going forward. Trump, Zelenskyy and al-Sharaa also held a short trilateral meeting on the sidelines.
global.geopolitical: Rescinding a nearly five-decade-old terrorism designation for a government led by a former insurgent commander the US once had a bounty on marks one of the fastest normalisations in recent US Middle East policy, and folds Syria into the same Ankara summit that dealt with Turkey's sanctions relief — recasting Damascus as an emerging NATO-adjacent partner rather than a pariah state, even as the Iran and Lebanon/Gaza fronts covered elsewhere in this briefing show how unstable the wider region remains.
global.socioeconomic: If Congress does not act to block it within the review period, SST rescission would open Syria to international trade, investment and reconstruction financing that has been unavailable for decades — a potentially significant reconstruction-financing story to watch, though with no direct Singapore angle yet.

global.headline: UK LABOUR LEADERSHIP CONTEST OPENS, BURNHAM ON COURSE FOR DOWNING STREET
summary: Nominations opened July 9 in the contest to succeed Keir Starmer as Labour leader and UK prime minister, following Starmer's resignation announcement in June after poor May local-election results and mounting pressure from Labour MPs amid the rise of Reform UK. Greater Manchester mayor Andy Burnham — who won a by-election in Makerfield in June specifically to secure a Commons seat — is so far the only declared candidate; getting on the ballot requires nomination by at least 20% of the Parliamentary Labour Party, or 81 MPs.

Labour MPs nominate from July 9-15, with affiliated organisations nominating July 15-16. If Burnham stands unopposed, he becomes Labour leader the day nominations close and is expected to become prime minister after seeing King Charles III around July 20. A contested race would instead go to a full members' ballot, with results due August 29.
global.geopolitical: A UK leadership change this close to NATO's Ukraine commitments and the Iran-driven Gulf crisis introduces some continuity uncertainty for Britain's posture on both, though Burnham is not expected to reverse commitments Labour has already made as a governing party — the transition is a domestic political story more than a foreign-policy pivot for now.
global.socioeconomic: Limited direct bearing on Singapore; UK leadership transitions mainly matter here for continuity of the UK-Singapore trade relationship and the countries' substantial mutual investment ties.

singapore.headline: 1.5 MILLION SINGAPOREANS TO GET UP TO $850 GSTV CASH, 710,000 SENIORS UP TO $450 MEDISAVE TOP-UP IN AUGUST
summary: The Ministry of Finance said 1.5 million adult Singaporeans will receive up to S$850 in GST Voucher – Cash in August 2026, with the amount depending on Assessable Income for Year of Assessment 2025 and the Annual Value of their residence. About 710,000 eligible Singaporean seniors will also receive up to S$450 in GSTV – MediSave top-ups (ranging S$150-S$450 by age and AV), credited automatically to CPF MediSave Accounts. Total disbursement under both schemes is about S$1.4 billion.
Recipients already signed up will receive payments automatically from August 7; citizens who have not signed up can do so by July 14 to receive payment in August.
singapore.geopolitical: Domestic fiscal matter with no external dimension.
singapore.socioeconomic: A routine annual scheme rather than a new stimulus response, but its timing lands against record COE premiums, a record Q3 electricity tariff and the inflationary risk from the Iran crisis's oil-price effects — all tracked elsewhere in this briefing — reinforcing how much of the cost-of-living picture now rests on scheduled transfers rather than price relief.

singapore.headline: GOVERNMENT UNVEILS DRIVER-TRANSITION PACKAGE FOR TAXI, PRIVATE-HIRE SECTOR AHEAD OF AUTONOMOUS-VEHICLE ROLLOUT
summary: Senior Minister of State for Transport Sun Xueling announced a new manpower transition package at the July 7 Future of Transport motion debate in Parliament, to help point-to-point (taxi and private-hire) drivers adapt as Singapore progressively adopts autonomous-vehicle (AV) technology. It has three components: Career Conversion Programmes offering employers up to 90% salary support during reskilling; a pilot Training Incentive Scheme, running from January 2027, paying S$20 an hour up to 80 hours (up to S$1,600 per driver) across roughly 2,000 SkillsFuture Workforce Development Agency-supported courses; and enhanced outreach and career guidance. Drivers can also train for AV-sector roles such as safety operator, remote operator and fleet management.

Strides Premier chief executive Ang Wei Neng welcomed the package but urged the Government to weigh salary and job-flexibility impacts more directly, warning that if AVs were to replace even 10% of the combined taxi/private-hire fleet, about 7,000 drivers could be displaced.
singapore.geopolitical: Domestic policy matter with no external dimension.
singapore.socioeconomic: Pre-empts labour disruption from AV adoption in a sector already squeezed by record COE premiums and the July 1 PARF rebate cut; the roughly 7,000-driver displacement estimate is the clearest public figure yet on the scale of the transition the package is meant to cushion.

singapore.headline: SINGAPORE LAUNCHES SIMFONI, A NATIONAL AI MODEL TRAINED ON LOCAL CLINICAL DATA
summary: Health Minister Ong Ye Kung announced the Singapore Medical Foundation AI Model (SIMFONI) initiative on July 9, an effort to build AI models trained on local clinical data and guidelines rather than the Western-population datasets most healthcare AI foundation models rely on. The initial focus is cardiometabolic conditions and eye disease, with eventual integration into the national electronic medical records system planned. The models are positioned as clinical decision-support "companions" — suggesting possible diagnoses, treatment pathways and next steps — rather than a replacement for clinicians, addressing pressure on the healthcare system from an ageing population, a rising chronic-disease burden and a stretched clinical workforce.
singapore.geopolitical: Part of a broader push toward sovereign, locally-trained AI infrastructure rather than reliance solely on foreign foundation models — a theme that also surfaced in Temasek's stated ambition, reported in yesterday's briefing, to raise its AI portfolio exposure to as much as 15% by 2031.
singapore.socioeconomic: A genuinely new, locally-trained clinical AI tool aimed at easing workforce strain in a healthcare system already facing demographic and chronic-disease pressure; longer-term implications for diagnostic accuracy and care costs will depend on how quickly it moves from pilot to the national EMR system.

word.definition: A complete reversal of position, opinion, or policy — especially one carried out abruptly, with little acknowledgment of the prior stance.
word.etymology: Borrowed via French volte-face, from Italian volta faccia ("turn face") — volta ("turn," from voltare) + faccia ("face"); entered English in early-19th-century diplomatic and military writing to describe an army, or a policy, wheeling round to face the opposite direction.
word.example: Trump sitting down with Ahmed al-Sharaa in Ankara and notifying Congress of his intent to strike Syria from the state-sponsors-of-terrorism list — a designation in place since 1979 — is as complete a volte-face as US policy toward Damascus has managed in a generation, arriving the same week Trump was threatening to seize an Iranian island outright.
